Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
I try to erase the memory of the event
I think about why the event has happened to me

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For chronic physical abuse by a romantic partner, being triggered by male presence and related people is coherent, but explosion/bang sounds points toward combat, accidents, or blast-related trauma and is hard to reconcile as a core trigger here without any matching assault-context cue elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: The rest of the profile reflects fear, avoidance, hypervigilance, fragmented memory, and negative self/world appraisals. Endorsing risky behavior pulls in the opposite direction and is not supported by other selected items; it reads as a different coping/symptom pattern than the otherwise strongly avoidant-threat profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: A marked loss of connection to community and culture is not well anchored to the rest of this intimate-partner-violence profile. The other appraisals center on danger, contamination, and shattered beliefs, but nothing else suggests cultural/community rupture, making this item feel clinically disconnected rather than tightly linked to the stated trauma formulation.

Clinical Vignette: Margaret

Margaret Kowalski is an eighty-year-old Polish-American woman who has spent the last fifty-three years as a clinical social worker, first in hospital settings and latterly in community mental health. She came to her first appointment in early November, referred by her primary care physician after Margaret disclosed to him that she had not slept properly in six weeks. Her PCL-5 score of 66 placed her firmly in the severe range for PTSD, though she had never named it as such until now.

The trauma itself occurred when Margaret was twenty-seven years old. She had been engaged to Thomas, a man she had known since childhood through Polish community circles in Pittsburgh. They had been together for four years when, in the spring of 1971, an argument about wedding plans escalated in his apartment. Thomas had been drinking. When Margaret said she wanted to postpone the wedding, he struck her across the face, then again, then threw her against the kitchen counter. The sequence of it remained fractured in her mind-not a coherent narrative but a series of isolated, vivid snapshots: his hand raised, the sound of her own cry, the cold edge of the countertop against her ribs, his voice saying things she could no longer recall in order. What stayed with her most vividly was the moment the door to his apartment swung open behind him as neighbors came to help her; the sudden intrusion of light and voices, and Thomas's silhouette in the doorway. She had left him that day and never returned.

For decades, Margaret had managed. She had built a career helping others, married briefly to a gentle man who died in 1989, and created a life of deliberate structure. But in recent months, something had shifted. She had begun to notice that she could not enter a room without immediately identifying the exits-a habit so ingrained she had stopped thinking of it as unusual until her colleague at the community center mentioned it. She found herself avoiding situations where she might be alone with male clients, redirecting appointments to younger female social workers with explanations that felt increasingly thin. She had taken to sleeping in her living room because the bedroom felt too enclosed, too far from the front door. When she did sleep, nightmares came-not full dreams but flashes, the same snapshots repeating. She had begun avoiding the hours just before dusk, when she knew sleep might come, staying up instead watching television until exhaustion forced her under.

What had finally compelled her to seek help was an incident at the senior center where she volunteers. A male volunteer, a kind man named Robert whom she had known for two years, had come up behind her to ask about a filing system. When he placed his hand on her shoulder, Margaret had flinched so violently that she knocked over a stack of folders. Robert had apologized profusely, confused by her reaction. In that moment, standing among scattered papers, Margaret had felt the full weight of what had happened to her-not as history, but as a present, inescapable fact.

She had come to believe, over the decades, that the world was fundamentally unsafe, that people could not be trusted no matter how long you knew them or how gentle they appeared. The attack had shattered her sense of how the world worked. She felt contaminated by what Thomas had done to her, as though the violence had left something permanent and dirty on her skin that no amount of time could wash away. She found herself thinking obsessively about why it had happened-what she had said or done that had provoked him, what she might have done differently. These thoughts offered no answers, only a cycling sense of culpability that she knew, intellectually, was irrational, but which felt absolutely true.

Margaret sits in the consulting room with her hands folded in her lap, her silver hair neatly pinned, her posture impeccable. She is articulate and reflective, a woman accustomed to observing human suffering in others. But her eyes are exhausted, and there is a tremor in her voice when she speaks about the sleeplessness, about the way her body now betrays her by reacting to men she consciously knows mean no harm. She is afraid that at eighty, she has run out of time to heal from this, that the trauma has simply waited all these years for her defenses to weaken. What she hopes for, though she barely dares to say it, is that she might be able to be alone in a room again without her body flooding with alarm.
